subject: cs
book: Computer Science Textbook for Class XI (NCERT)

concepts.text: A computer as an electronic device that takes input, processes it under program control and produces output
Block diagram of a computer: input unit, CPU, memory, output unit, storage, and the data flow between them
CPU parts: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), Control Unit (CU) and registers, and the role of each
Input devices and their use (keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, touch screen, biometric/sensor devices)
Output devices and their use (monitor, printer, speaker, projector, 3D printer)
Hardware versus software; computers ranging from servers and desktops to laptops, tablets and smartphones
Early calculating aids: abacus, Pascaline, Leibniz's machine
Babbage's Analytical Engine and the idea of a programmable machine; Hollerith's punched cards
Von Neumann stored-program architecture (program and data held in memory)
Generations of computers: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, VLSI/microprocessors
Arrival of personal computers, laptops, mobile devices and today's trends (wearables, IoT, AI)
Why a computer needs memory to hold data and instructions
Units of memory: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) and conversions between them
Primary memory: RAM (volatile, read-write) versus ROM (non-volatile, holds boot instructions)
Cache memory as a small, fast memory between CPU and RAM that holds frequently used data
Secondary memory: permanent, larger, slower storage (HDD, SSD, CD/DVD, pen drive, memory card)
Comparing primary and secondary memory by speed, cost, capacity and volatility (memory hierarchy)

sections.name: 1.4 Data Transfer between Memory and CPU

concepts.text: System bus as the set of wires that carries data between CPU, memory and I/O
Data bus (bidirectional, carries data), address bus (unidirectional, carries memory addresses) and control bus (carries control signals)
Microprocessor as a CPU built on a single chip; growth from early chips to multi-core processors
Microprocessor specifications: word size, memory size (addressable memory), clock speed (Hz), number of cores
Microcontroller as a small computer on a chip (CPU, memory, I/O) used in embedded devices like washing machines and remotes
Data as raw facts versus information as processed, meaningful data
Types of data: structured (tables), unstructured (images, audio, free text) and semi-structured (email, HTML, XML)
Data capturing, storage and retrieval: input devices, storage media and accessing stored data
Data deletion (moving to recycle bin, permanent deletion) and data recovery, and the privacy risk of recoverable deleted data
Need for software: hardware works only through sets of instructions (programs)
System software: operating system, system utilities (antivirus, disk cleanup, backup) and device drivers
Programming languages: low-level (machine language, assembly language) versus high-level languages
Language translators: assembler, compiler (whole program at once) and interpreter (line by line); compiler versus interpreter
Program development tools: text editors and IDEs
Application software: general-purpose (word processor, spreadsheet, browser) versus customised/specific-purpose (payroll, booking systems)
Proprietary software versus free and open-source software (FOSS) and freeware
Operating system as the interface between user and hardware that manages resources
OS user interfaces: command-based, graphical (GUI), touch-based, voice-based and gesture-based
Functions of an OS: process management, memory management, file management, device management
Exercise types: differentiate RAM/ROM, compiler/interpreter, system/application software; memory unit conversions; name bus types and OS functions
Encoding as mapping each key or character to a unique code that is stored in binary
Example: key 'A' maps to decimal 65; a Devanagari letter maps to a hexadecimal Unicode value
Encoding versus encryption (encryption hides data; encoding represents it)

sections.name: 2.1.1 American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII)

concepts.text: ASCII as a 7-bit code representing 128 characters (English letters, digits, symbols, control codes)
Encoding a word into ASCII decimal codes and 7-bit binary (e.g. 'DATA', 'COMPUTER')
Limitation: ASCII cannot represent Indian or other non-English scripts

sections.name: 2.1.2 Indian Script Code for Information Interchange (ISCII)

concepts.text: ISCII as an 8-bit code (256 characters) for Indian scripts that keeps the first 128 ASCII codes
Indian aksharas placed in the upper code range (160-255)
Unicode as a universal standard giving every character of every script a unique number
Unicode encodings UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 and why UTF-32 uses more space
Unicode as a superset of ASCII; reading the Devanagari Unicode table
Advantages of Unicode for Indian-language content and how to type in Unicode (activity: Unicode fonts for Indian languages)
Positional number system: a digit's value depends on its position; radix (base) = number of symbols
Writing the base as a subscript (e.g. 70 base 8 vs 70 base 10) and positional expansion including fractions

sections.name: 2.2.1-2.2.4 Decimal, Binary, Octal and Hexadecimal Number Systems

concepts.text: Decimal system: base 10, digits 0-9
Binary system: base 2, digits 0 and 1, linked to ON/OFF states of transistors
Octal system: base 8, digits 0-7; each octal digit equals 3 bits
Hexadecimal system: base 16, symbols 0-9 and A-F; each hex digit equals 4 bits
Hex used to write memory addresses compactly
Hex RGB colour codes (24-bit, e.g. red = FF0000) for web and graphics

sections.name: 2.3.1 Conversion from Decimal to other Number Systems

concepts.text: Decimal to binary by repeated division by 2, reading remainders bottom-up
Decimal to octal by repeated division by 8
Decimal to hexadecimal by repeated division by 16 (remainders 10-15 written as A-F)

sections.name: 2.3.2 Conversion from other Number Systems to Decimal

concepts.text: Binary to decimal by multiplying each bit by its power of 2 and adding
Octal to decimal using powers of 8
Hexadecimal to decimal using powers of 16

sections.name: 2.3.3 Conversion from Binary to Octal/Hexadecimal and vice versa

concepts.text: Binary to octal by grouping bits in threes from the right (padding with leading zeros)
Octal to binary by writing each octal digit as 3 bits
Binary to hexadecimal by grouping bits in fours; hexadecimal to binary by writing each digit as 4 bits
Octal to hexadecimal (and reverse) via binary

sections.name: 2.3.4 Conversion of a Number with Fractional Part

concepts.text: Decimal fraction to binary/octal/hex by repeated multiplication by the base, reading integer parts top-down
When to stop: fraction becomes 0, starts repeating, or after a fixed number of steps
Non-decimal fraction to decimal using negative powers of the base (e.g. 100101.101 base 2)
Fractional binary to octal/hex by grouping bits outward from the binary point
Exercise types: base values, full forms, mixed conversions with and without fractions, ASCII/Unicode encoding of words

sections.name: Boolean Logic (CBSE syllabus topic, not printed in the NCERT chapter)

concepts.text: Boolean values (True/False, 1/0) and Boolean variables
Basic logic operations and gates: NOT, AND, OR with symbols and truth tables
Derived gates NAND, NOR and XOR with symbols and truth tables
Building truth tables for Boolean expressions with two or three variables
De Morgan's laws: NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B, NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B, and verifying them by truth table
Drawing logic circuits for a given Boolean expression and writing the expression for a given circuit
Computers solve problems only when given precise step-by-step instructions (e.g. online ticket booking)
Problem solving as identifying a problem, designing a solution and implementing it as a program
Analysing the problem: understand inputs, outputs and requirements
Developing an algorithm: plan the solution in steps before coding
Coding: translate the algorithm into a programming language
Testing and debugging: run with test data, find and fix errors; kinds of testing (unit, integration, system, acceptance)
Algorithm as a finite, ordered set of exact steps with a clear start and end
Why algorithms are needed: clarity, correctness, communication of the solution before coding
Characteristics of a good algorithm: precision, uniqueness of steps, finiteness, defined input and output
Flowchart as a visual representation; standard symbols: terminator, process, decision, input/output, arrow/flow line
Drawing flowcharts for simple problems (sum of two numbers, square of a number, largest of numbers)
Pseudocode as an informal, language-neutral description using keywords like INPUT, COMPUTE, PRINT, IF/ELSE, WHILE
Writing pseudocode for given tasks; benefits of pseudocode
Sequence: steps executed one after another
Selection: choosing between alternatives using conditions (if-else), e.g. checking odd/even or age eligibility
Repetition (iteration): repeating steps while a condition holds, e.g. summing numbers or counting
Dry run: tracing an algorithm by hand with sample inputs to check correctness
Choosing test inputs including boundary and special cases
Several algorithms can solve the same problem (e.g. ways to check if a number is prime)
Comparing algorithms by time (processing steps) and space (memory) needed
Source code written in a high-level language following its syntax
Translating source code to machine code through a compiler or interpreter
Decomposition: breaking a complex problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved independently
Real-life decomposition examples (railway reservation system, school management) and benefits like team division
Exercise types: write algorithm/pseudocode/flowchart for given tasks, dry-run algorithms, identify flow-of-control type, decompose a problem
Program and programming language; Python as a high-level, interpreted, open-source language
Features of Python: simple syntax, free and open source, interpreted, portable, case-sensitive, rich library, uses indentation
Working with Python: the interpreter/IDLE shell and the >>> prompt
Execution modes: interactive mode versus script mode (.py files); running a first 'Hello World' program

sections.name: Python character set and tokens (CBSE syllabus)

concepts.text: Python character set: letters, digits, special symbols, whitespace
Tokens: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators
Keywords as reserved words with special meaning (e.g. if, else, for, True, None) that cannot be used as names
Rules for naming identifiers: start with a letter or underscore, no special symbols or spaces, not a keyword, case-sensitive
Identifying valid and invalid identifiers; choosing meaningful names
Variable as a name referring to a value in memory; no explicit declaration needed
Assignment with = and multiple assignment; l-value and r-value
Comments with # (single line) and their role in readability; docstrings
Every value is an object with identity, type and value; id() returns its identity
Number types: int, float, complex; bool as a subtype of int
Sequence types: string, list and tuple
Set type (unordered, unique elements) and None (absence of value)
Mapping type: dictionary of key-value pairs
Mutable (list, dictionary, set) versus immutable (int, float, string, tuple) types and what happens on reassignment
Deciding which data type to use for a given situation; type() to check type
Arithmetic operators: + - * / % // ** and their results with int and float
Relational operators: == != > < >= <= giving Boolean results
Assignment and augmented assignment operators: = += -= *= /= %= //= **=
Logical operators: and, or, not, and truth values of non-Boolean operands
Identity operators: is, is not (compare object identity)
Membership operators: in, not in (test presence in a sequence)
Expression as a combination of values, variables and operators that evaluates to a value
Precedence and associativity of operators (** is right-associative); evaluating expressions step by step
Statement as a unit of code that Python executes; expression versus statement
input() reads a string from the user, with an optional prompt
print() displays output; sep and end parameters
Programs: area/perimeter, simple interest, temperature conversion, swapping values
Explicit conversion (type casting) with int(), float(), str(), chr(), ord() and errors from invalid conversion
Implicit conversion (coercion), e.g. int + float gives float
Debugging as finding and removing errors (bugs)
Syntax errors: breaking the language rules
Logical errors: program runs but gives wrong output
Runtime errors: program stops during execution (e.g. division by zero, invalid input)
Exercise types: valid identifiers, evaluate expressions, predict output, identify error type, write small programs
Flow of control as the order in which statements execute
Three structures: sequential, conditional (selection) and iterative (repetition)
if statement syntax and flowchart
if-else statement for two-way choice
if-elif-else ladder for multi-way choice
Nested if statements
Programs: absolute value, larger of two numbers, sorting three numbers, divisibility check, positive/negative/zero
Programs: simple calculator with menu, traffic-signal action, grade from marks, leap year
Indentation (usually 4 spaces) defines a block in Python; IndentationError when inconsistent
Need for loops to repeat a set of statements
for loop over a sequence (string, list, range) and its flowchart
range(start, stop, step) function, including negative steps and default values
Programs: print numbers/even numbers, multiplication table, sum of first n numbers
while loop with a condition and loop variable update; flowchart
Infinite loops and how to avoid them
Programs: factorial of a number, sum of digits, reverse a number, HCF/GCD
break: exit the loop immediately
continue: skip the rest of the current iteration
else clause with loops (runs when loop ends without break)
pass statement as a placeholder
Programs: check prime number using break, skip specific values using continue
A loop inside another loop and how inner iterations run for each outer iteration
Pattern programs: star/number triangles and pyramids
Programs: prime numbers in a range, summation of series (e.g. 1 + x + x^2 + ...)
Exercise types: predict output, convert for to while, trace loop count, write programs with conditions and loops
String as a sequence of Unicode characters enclosed in single, double or triple quotes; multi-line strings
Accessing characters by index: positive (from 0) and negative (from -1) indexing
IndexError for out-of-range index; index must be an integer
Strings are immutable: characters cannot be changed in place (TypeError)
Concatenation with +
Repetition with *
Membership with in and not in
Slicing str[m:n], with step str[m:n:k], omitted indices and negative indices; reversing with [::-1]
Traversal using a for loop over characters
Traversal using a while loop with an index and len()
len() for length
Case methods: title(), lower(), upper(), capitalize(), swapcase()
count() and find() (returns -1 if absent) and index() (raises error if absent)
startswith() and endswith()
Testing methods: isalnum(), isalpha(), isdigit(), islower(), isupper(), isspace(), istitle()
Whitespace removal: lstrip(), rstrip(), strip()
replace(), join(), partition() and split()
Program: count occurrences of a character in a string
Program: replace all vowels with a symbol
Program: reverse a string without slicing
Program: check whether a string is a palindrome
Programs: count vowels/consonants/uppercase/lowercase/digits/words; menu-driven string operations
Exercise types: predict output of slicing and methods, write programs for string manipulation
List as an ordered, mutable sequence of possibly mixed-type elements in square brackets
Accessing elements with positive and negative indices
Lists are mutable: change elements by index assignment
Concatenation with + (both operands must be lists)
Repetition with *
Membership with in and not in
Slicing, including steps, negative indices and reversing
Traversal with for loop over elements and with range(len()) / while loop by index
len() and list() constructor (from string, tuple, range)
Adding elements: append(), extend(), insert()
count() and index()
Removing elements: remove(), pop() (with/without index), del statement, clear()
reverse() and sort() (with reverse=True) which change the list in place
sorted() which returns a new sorted list
min(), max() and sum() on numeric lists
A list containing lists; accessing elements with two indices like L[i][j]
Assignment creates an alias (both names refer to same list)
True copies using slicing [:], list() or copy() method/copy module
Changes made to a list inside a function affect the original (mutability)
Reassigning the parameter inside a function does not change the original list
Menu-driven program to perform list operations (append, insert, delete, modify, sort, display)
Program: find maximum, minimum and mean of numbers in a list
Program: linear search for an element in a list and report its position
Program: count frequency of elements in a list
Exercise types: predict output of list operations, write list-processing programs
Tuple as an ordered, immutable sequence in parentheses; single-element tuple needs a trailing comma
Accessing tuple elements with positive/negative indexing
Tuples are immutable, but a mutable element inside a tuple (e.g. a list) can change
When to prefer tuples over lists (fixed data, faster iteration)
Concatenation, repetition, membership and slicing on tuples
len(), tuple(), count(), index()
sorted() (returns a list), min(), max(), sum()
Unpacking a tuple into variables; swapping values with tuple assignment
Count of variables must match tuple length (ValueError otherwise)
Tuple within a tuple; e.g. storing student records and printing them
Programs: swap two numbers, compute area/circumference returning a tuple, find min/max/mean of tuple values
Programs: linear search in a tuple, frequency of elements in a tuple
Dictionary as a mutable mapping of unique, immutable keys to values in braces
Creating dictionaries with {} and dict()
Accessing values using keys; KeyError for missing keys
Adding a new key-value pair
Modifying the value of an existing key
Membership test with in / not in (checks keys)
Traversing a dictionary with for loop over keys and over items()
len(), dict(), keys(), values(), items()
get() (safe access with default) and update() (merge another dictionary)
del statement and clear()
fromkeys(), copy(), pop(), popitem(), setdefault() (CBSE syllabus)
max(), min() and sorted() applied to dictionary keys
Program: count how many times each character appears in a string using a dictionary
Program: store employee names and salaries, then access/update them
Program: convert a number into words using a digit-to-word dictionary; marks/record lookups

sections.name: Introduction to Python Modules (from NCERT Functions chapter 7.5, per CBSE syllabus)

concepts.text: Module as a .py file of reusable functions; Python standard library
Importing with import module_name and calling module.function()
Importing selected items with from module import name (and from module import *)
math module: pi, e, sqrt(), ceil(), floor(), pow(), fabs(), sin(), cos(), tan(); also factorial(), gcd(), fmod()
Difference between built-in pow() and math.pow() (float result)
random module: random(), randint(a, b), randrange(start, stop, step)
statistics module: mean(), median(), mode()
Exercise types: predict output of tuple/dictionary code, write programs using dictionaries and modules
Digital technology makes life faster and easier but can also be misused
Digital footprint as the trail of data left online
Active footprints (posts, emails) versus passive footprints (browsing data, cookies, location)
Footprints are stored by browsers and servers and are hard to erase
Digital society and the netizen as a responsible digital citizen
Net etiquettes: be ethical (no copyright violation, share expertise), be respectful (privacy, diversity), be responsible (avoid cyberbullying, don't feed trolls)
Communication etiquettes: be precise, respect time and data limits, be polite, be credible; avoid spam
Social media etiquettes: be secure (strong passwords, unknown friends, fake news), be reliable (think before uploading)
Protecting sensitive personal data through encryption, authentication and data-protection laws
Intellectual Property Rights: copyright, patent (about 20 years) and trademark
Violation of IPR: plagiarism, copyright infringement, trademark infringement
Public access and open-source software: Creative Commons, GNU GPL and Apache licences; FOSS; software piracy
Cyber crime as crime using a computer as tool or target
Hacking: ethical (white hat) versus non-ethical (black hat) hacking
Phishing, fraud emails, email spoofing and identity theft (financial, criminal, medical)
Ransomware: encrypting data and demanding payment; how it spreads
Eavesdropping, cyber trolls and cyber bullying (CBSE syllabus)
Combatting and preventing cyber crime: backups, antivirus, updates, strong passwords, HTTPS sites, digital signatures, reporting to cyber cell
Cyber safety: safely browsing the web, identity protection, maintaining confidentiality
Malware types: viruses, trojans, adware (and worms, spyware) and their effects
IT Act 2000 (amended 2008): legal recognition of electronic records and digital signatures
Provisions against cyber crimes, cyber cells and the Cyber Appellate Tribunal
E-waste: discarded electronic devices and their harmful effects on health and environment
Proper disposal: reduce, reuse, recycle and authorised e-waste collection
Health effects of overuse: eye strain, poor posture, repetitive stress, internet addiction
Ergonomics and good device-care habits
Gender and disability issues while teaching and using computers; assistive and inclusive technology
Exercise types: scenario-based classification (plagiarism, hacking, fraud), differences (copyright vs patent), etiquette analysis, IT Act provisions
